+# Design — Tic-Tac-Toe, No Draws
+
+This document is the brief's design deliverable. It records how the brief was read, the rule sets
+that were considered and rejected, the argument that a Draw is impossible and that play always
+terminates, how Balance is claimed and bounded, and what is known to be broken or unfinished.
+
+The rule lives only in [RULES.md](RULES.md); this document does not define or alter it, and where it
+must name the decision it links to [ADR-0001](adr/0001-lineless-full-board-awarded-to-o.md). The
+numbers cited below are from [research/no-draw-variants.md](research/no-draw-variants.md), which
+also contains the exhaustive solver that reproduces them. Domain terms carry the meanings given in
+[CONTEXT.md](../CONTEXT.md), the project glossary.
+
+## 1. Reading of the brief
+
+The brief asks for a two-player tic-tac-toe **variant** in which (MUST) every **Terminal** position
+has a winner, and (MUST) no line of play continues indefinitely, while remaining recognisably
+tic-tac-toe: a 3×3 grid, two players, X and O, alternating turns. It fixes the medium
+(HTML/CSS/JS, no build step, no backend, no network calls, current Chrome) and the deliverables
+(game, `docs/RULES.md`, `docs/DESIGN.md`, commit history, `transcript/`), and it deliberately
+leaves the interesting parts open.
+
+We read "variant" as: keep standard tic-tac-toe and change as little as possible, because the
+constraint that carries the risk is "recognisably tic-tac-toe", not originality (the brief says the
+rule need not be original). So the design problem is not "invent a game"; it is "keep the standard
+game and eliminate its one non-winning outcome, the Draw".
+
+### Ambiguities found and how they were resolved
+
+1. **What is a Draw, and when does a game end?** The brief forbids "a terminal state in which
+   neither player has won" but never says what makes a position Terminal. We read it as: a game
+   ends only when a Line win or a Fill win occurs, and every such position names a winner; a Draw
+   is therefore a Terminal position with no winner, and must be unreachable. Recorded in
+   [CONTEXT.md](../CONTEXT.md) (**Draw**, **Terminal**) and enforced by the engine having no draw
+   outcome.
+2. **The lineless full Board.** Standard tic-tac-toe's only non-winning Terminal positions are the
+   16 full Boards with no Line (46,080 of 255,168 lines of play, 18.06%). Any variant that keeps
+   the standard Line win must decide who gets them. This is the pivotal ambiguity and is resolved
+   in ADR-0001: they are awarded to O. Because X moves first and nine is odd, the ninth move is
+   always X's, so "the Board fills with no Line, O wins" is equivalently "the ninth move loses".
+3. **A ninth move that both completes a Line and fills the Board.** The brief does not say which
+   rule wins. Resolved as a Line win for its mover, so the Fill win can never steal an earned Line
+   win. This is the only interaction between the two winning conditions; it is stated in
+   [RULES.md](RULES.md) and encoded in the engine's status order (Line checked before the fill
+   test).
+4. **Must the variant be balanced?** The brief never mentions Balance; it asks only that every
+   game have a winner. We treated Balance as a discretionary quality goal, not a requirement, and
+   only insofar as it could be measured cheaply from the same exhaustive analysis. Section 4
+   states exactly how weak the claim is.
+5. **"Always terminates": structural or probabilistic?** The brief does not distinguish. Resolved
+   structurally: a move occupies a previously empty cell, with no passing, capture, or removal, so
+   the game cannot revisit a position and cannot exceed nine moves. No random device or tiebreak is
+   used, so termination does not depend on chance.
+6. **Where do decisions get recorded?** The brief asks that decisions and reasoning be recorded but
+   does not say where. We split it: ADR-0001 for the one decision that a future reader would
+   question, the research note for the evidence behind it, and this document for the combined
+   reading. `docs/RULES.md` states only the playable rule.
+7. **Match length, passing, moving or removing Marks.** The brief leaves these open. Resolved in
+   the conventional way: place one Mark per turn, no passing, no moving, no removal, first Line
+   wins.
+8. **A computer opponent.** Explicitly optional and unscored. Declined; the game is human vs
+   human.
+9. **Deliverables outside the game.** `transcript/` and per-boundary commit history are brief
+   requirements but are process rather than rule design, so they are handled as commits and as
+   transcript files (see Section 5 for the one piece still outstanding).
+
+## 2. Rule sets considered and rejected
+
+The rule sets and their measured numbers are the research note's comparison table
+([research/no-draw-variants.md §1](research/no-draw-variants.md)). Every number below is exact, from
+exhaustive enumeration of the complete game tree (all 255,168 standard lines of play), not a
+sample or a simulation. "Move-uniform" is the exact random-play probability split; "leaves" is the
+share of terminal sequences; "greedy" is the exact split under win-or-block-then-random play;
+"perfect" is the minimax value.
+
+| # | Rule (delta from standard) | Draws? | Max len | Perfect | Move-uniform X/O | Leaves X/O | Greedy X/O | Verdict |
+|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
+| — | Standard: own Line wins; lineless full Board is a draw | yes | 9 | draw | 58.5 / 28.8 | 51.4 / 30.5 | 31.1 / 17.4 | reject: 46,080 Draws |
+| A | lineless full Board awarded to the last mover (X) | no | 9 | X, every opening | 71.2 / 28.8 | 69.5 / 30.5 | 82.6 / 17.4 | simplest fix, but lopsided |
+| **B** | **lineless full Board awarded to the other player (O)** | **no** | **9** | **O, no winning opening** | **58.5 / 41.5** | **51.4 / 48.6** | **31.1 / 68.9** | **chosen (ADR-0001)** |
+| C | misère (own Line loses) + full Board to the last mover | no | 9 | X, centre only | 41.5 / 58.5 | 48.6 / 51.4 | 26.5 / 73.5 | balanced, but longer wording and a known forced X win |
+| D | misère + full Board to the other player | no | 9 | O, no winning opening | 28.8 / 71.2 | 30.5 / 69.5 | 13.7 / 86.3 | reject: dominated by B |
+| E | a move wins by fully occupying any Line, whatever the symbols | no | 7 | X, every opening | 51.6 / 48.4 | 44.6 / 55.4 | 100 / 0 | reject: unintuitive, brittle under simple play |
+| F(i) | O pre-placed on the centre + full Board to the last mover | no | 8 | O, no winning opening | 19.3 / 80.7 | 21.7 / 78.3 | 4.2 / 95.8 | reject: badly O-dominant |
+| F(ii) | O pre-placed on the centre + full Board to the other player | no | 8 | X, corners only | 30.7 / 69.3 | 39.5 / 60.5 | 70.0 / 30.0 | reject: handicap does not balance |
+| G | Maker–Breaker: X wins a Line, O wins a filled Board with no X Line | no by definition | 9 | X, centre and corners | 77.8 / 22.2 | 71.0 / 29.0 | 34.1 / 65.9 | viable, but asymmetric goals |
+| H | Notakto: both players place X; completing a Line loses | no | 7 | first, centre only | 48.4 / 51.6 | 55.4 / 44.6 | 62.8 / 37.2 | simplest and best casual balance, but single-symbol |
+
+Two notes on reading the table. The standard row is the baseline, not a candidate, and its greedy
+and leaf columns omit the Draw share (51.5% and 18.1% respectively). H's two players are "first"
+and "second" rather than X and O, because both players place the same symbol.
+
+The reasoning behind the choice, in the terms ADR-0001 uses:
+
+- The brief's only hard requirement is "no Draw". Rule A is the smallest possible change that
+  achieves it, but awarding the lineless board to the player who moved last gives it to X and
+  makes X win 69.5% of lines of play with every opening a forced X win. Rejected as lopsided.
+- **Rule B** (the chosen rule) resolves the same ambiguity in the opposite direction. It is one
+  sentence, no Draws, terminates by nine, and is the closest to even under both casual measures
+  (leaves 51.4 / 48.6; move-uniform 58.5 / 41.5). Its cost is that it hands the forced win to O
+  under perfect play, and that competent (greedy) play steers games to filled Boards, where O wins
+  68.9%. Section 4 explains why that cost is unavoidable and how it is bounded.
+- Rule C is the mirror image of B in casual balance, and misère is a well-known variant, but it
+  needs a longer sentence and gives X a short, teachable forced win (centre plus 180° mirror),
+  verified over all 360 O reply sequences.
+- D is B's forced winner (O) with much worse balance; B dominates it. The F variants add two rules
+  and the fill tiebreak still dominates the outcome; B dominates F(i) too.
+- E and G are no-Draw by construction but change the character of the game more than B: E allows a
+  mixed line to win and is degenerate under greedy play (X 100%), while G makes O unable to win by
+  a Line, which is no longer recognisably tic-tac-toe.
+- H has the simplest rule of all and the best casual balance, but it uses a single symbol and so
+  stretches "X and O alternating". The brief's recognition constraint rules it out.
+
+The one interpretation fixed by the research note that matters to the table: a move that both
+completes a Line and fills the Board is resolved as a Line result. This is also the interaction
+decision in Section 1, ambiguity 3.
+
+## 3. Why no Draw is possible, and why play always terminates
+
+**Termination.** Fix the starting position (empty **Board**, X to move). Every legal move places a
+Mark in a cell that was empty, and the rules provide no passing, no capture, no removal, and no way
+to move an existing Mark. The number of Marks on the Board therefore increases by exactly one on
+every move, from 0 towards at most 9. A strictly increasing integer cannot revisit a value, so no
+position repeats and no cycle exists: the state graph is a finite DAG graded by Mark count. Play
+therefore cannot continue past the ninth move. The research note's solver asserts, for every edge
+of every enumerated tree, that the child has exactly one more Mark than its parent, and terminated
+without any cycle or recursion guard for all candidates.
+
+**No Draw.** The rule ([RULES.md](RULES.md)) declares exactly two ways a game can end. In the
+first, a player completes a Line of their own Marks; the winner is that player, a **Line win**. In
+the second, the Board reaches nine Marks with no Line at all; the winner is O, a **Fill win**. Every
+position is therefore in exactly one of three cases:
+
+1. some Line is present — Terminal, and the winner is the player who completed it. At a reachable
+   position at most one Line exists, because play stops the moment the first Line appears, so the
+   winner is the player who has just moved;
+2. no Line, Board full — Terminal, winner is O;
+3. no Line, Board not full — not Terminal, and by the termination argument play continues.
+
+Cases 1 and 2 are the only Terminal positions, and each names a winner. A **Draw** would be a
+Terminal position in neither case 1 nor case 2, and there is no such case; the rule's end-of-game
+test is total and every branch of it assigns a winner. This is why the variant has no "draw"
+outcome to represent: it is not that Draws are merely rare, it is that the rule's Terminal test
+never produces one. The ninth-move precedence (ambiguity 3) matters here: a full Board that
+contains a Line is decided by case 1, so it is a Line win, not a Fill win — but either branch
+still has a winner.
+
+**The exhaustive check.** The informal argument above is about the rule; the research note is the
+machine-checked evidence that the rule, as interpreted, behaves this way over all play. The solver
+enumerates every legal sequence of moves for each candidate, stopping at Terminal positions, and
+reports for the chosen rule B ([§6](research/no-draw-variants.md)):
+
+- 255,168 terminal lines of play, split X 131,184 / O 123,984 / draw **0**;
+- maximum length **9** moves;
+- 5,478 distinct reachable (Board, turn) states, 549,946 nodes in the unfolded tree;
+- the 46,080 terminal lines of play that were Draws under the standard rule are reclassified as O
+  Fill wins, and all 16 distinct lineless full Boards are reachable in normal play.
+
+Because the tree is finite and fully enumerated, this is a statement about all play, not a sample:
+zero Draws and a maximum length of nine. The research note's standard baseline reproduces the
+classic counts (255,168; 131,184 / 77,904 / 46,080) exactly, which cross-checks the enumeration
+against the literature before it is trusted for the variant.
+
+## 4. Balance: what is claimed, and what is not
+
+**Perfect-play Balance is impossible in any no-Draw variant.** In a finite perfect-information game
+with no Draws, Zermelo determinacy says exactly one player has a forced win; the third outcome,
+"both can hold", requires Draws to exist. So a 50/50 perfect-play split cannot exist for any rule
+that satisfies the brief. Under the chosen rule, perfect play is an O win, and X has no winning
+opening (every one of the nine first moves has value O). That is not a defect of this rule; it is
+forced on every candidate ([research/no-draw-variants.md §3.6](research/no-draw-variants.md)).
+
+**Empirical Balance is claimed only under a named play policy.** The policy is *uniform random
+play*: each player chooses uniformly among the legal moves. Under that policy the chosen rule's
+outcome split is X **58.5%** / O **41.5%**, with no Draw. Under the alternative presentation, the
+share of terminal sequences, it is X **51.4%** / O **48.6%**. Neither figure is a claim about
+competent play, and the document deliberately does not make one:
+
+- Under a greedy policy (win if possible, otherwise block the opponent's immediate win, otherwise
+  move at random), the split is X **31.1%** / O **68.9%**: a player who knows only "win or block"
+  steers games to filled Boards, where the rule gives them to O. The variant must not be described
+  as balanced for competent play.
+- The three measures disagree because they weight long games differently; a reader judging
+  "balance" must say which distribution is meant. The move-uniform figure is the one a bored
+  human approximates; the greedy figure is the one a beginner approximates.
+
+In short: this variant is defended as *near-even for casual, near-random play*, and its perfect-play
+value is a forced O win, which is unavoidable. The swap (pie) rule was also checked and does not
+restore theoretical Balance: in a no-Draw game it moves the forced win to the second player
+([research/no-draw-variants.md §3.7](research/no-draw-variants.md)).
+
+## 5. Known broken or unfinished
+
+- **`transcript/README.md` is not written.** The brief asks for a short index of which tools and
+  models were used and which session file corresponds to which phase. The raw session files are
+  committed under `transcript/`, but the index that maps them to phases is still outstanding. This
+  is the one brief deliverable not yet complete.
+- **No automated verification at the engine seam.** By decision (spec, *Testing Decisions*), no
+  test runner is introduced. The no-Draw and termination argument above is informal prose plus the
+  research note's exhaustive enumeration, which is a check of the **rule**, not of the JavaScript
+  engine. The engine is a direct encoding of that rule, but nothing mechanically proves the two
+  stay in step. If rule/engine drift is ever suspected, the fix is the spec's seam test: walk every
+  line of play from `createGame()` via `legalMoves`/`applyMove` and assert every Terminal state has
+  a winner, `legalMoves` is empty at Terminal states, and no line of play exceeds nine moves.
+- **No computer opponent.** Explicitly optional and unscored by the brief; human vs human only.
+- **Visual polish and accessibility are minimal and consciously unscored.** The Board is rendered
+  plainly; a Line win highlights its three cells and a Fill win gets a distinct treatment (ticket
+  03), which is enough to make the variant visible. Responsive layout, animation, sound, and a full
+  accessibility pass were not attempted; the live status region and per-cell labels are the extent
+  of it and have not been audited.
+- **Time box.** The brief allows a maximum of three hours of *active* work. The only evidence the
+  repository can offer is commit timestamps: at the time of writing, the commits span 13:47 to 15:06
+  on 2026-09-21, about 1 hour 20 minutes of wall-clock, and active work is necessarily a subset of
+  that. On that evidence the box has not been exceeded; a reader who needs an exact active-work
+  figure should treat the commit timestamps and `transcript/` as the record, not this sentence.
+- **Issue tracker state is manual.** The tickets under `scratch/no-draw-tic-tac-toe/issues/` are
+  marked `ready-for-agent` and are not automatically flipped to done when the work lands.
+
+## 6. Document map
+
+- [RULES.md](RULES.md) — the rule, and the only authority for it.
+- [ADR-0001](adr/0001-lineless-full-board-awarded-to-o.md) — why the lineless full Board goes to O.
+- [research/no-draw-variants.md](research/no-draw-variants.md) — exhaustive enumeration of all
+  candidates, the comparison table, and the solver.
+- [CONTEXT.md](../CONTEXT.md) — the glossary this document and the code use.
+- [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md) — how to run the game and the engine/interface conventions.

# Tic-Tac-Toe, No Draws — Rules

Two players, **X** and **O**, take turns on a 3×3 grid. **X moves first.** On your turn, place
your mark in any empty square. You may not pass, move a mark, or remove one.

## Winning

The first player to get **three of their own marks in a straight line** — any row, column, or
diagonal — wins immediately.

## The no-draw rule

**If all nine squares are filled and neither player has three in a row, O wins.**

In other words: X must win outright. If X never completes a line, O wins, either by completing a
line of O's own or by the board filling up.

## End of the game

A game ends in exactly two ways:

1. A player completes a line of three — that player wins.
2. The board fills with no line — O wins.

Every game therefore ends in at most nine moves, and every game has a winner.

## Notes

- If the ninth (final) move completes a line, the line wins. The no-draw rule applies only when
  the board fills with no line at all.
- The board below is full with no line for either player, so O wins:

  ```
  X O X
  O O X
  X X O
  ```

1: # Tic-Tac-Toe, No Draws
2: 
3: A two-player tic-tac-toe variant whose entire reason to exist is that every game ends with a
4: winner: X moves first and must complete a line, and a board that fills with no line is awarded
5: to O.
6: 
7: ## Language
8: 
9: **Board**:
10: The 3×3 grid of nine cells; together with whose turn it is, the whole state of a game.
11: _Avoid_: Grid, field
12: 
13: **Mark**:
14: An X or an O occupying a cell. X always moves first, so X places on moves 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9, and
15: O on moves 2, 4, 6 and 8.
16: _Avoid_: Piece, token, stone
17: 
18: **Line**:
19: Any of the eight triples of cells — three rows, three columns, two diagonals — in which a line
20: win can be completed. Use "row", "column" and "diagonal" only when the orientation matters.
21: _Avoid_: Three-in-a-row (as a name for the cells themselves)
22: 
23: **Line win**:
24: A player wins by placing a mark that completes a line of three of their own marks.
25: _Avoid_: Normal win, standard win
26: 
27: **Fill win**:
28: O wins because the board reaches nine marks with no line. At most one fill win can occur in a
29: game, and it is always X that has just moved, so a fill win is equivalently "the ninth move
30: loses".
31: _Avoid_: Draw-tiebreak, board-full win, stalemate
32: 
33: **Draw**:
34: A terminal position with no winner. This variant exists to make draws unreachable; a draw is
35: never a runtime outcome and must never be presented as one.
36: _Avoid_: Tie, stalemate
37: 
38: **Terminal**:
39: A position in which the game has ended — by either a line win or a fill win.
40: 
41: **Balance**:
42: Closeness of the two players' win rates. Two senses must not be conflated: *perfect-play
43: balance* is impossible in any no-draw variant, because exactly one player has a forced win,
44: while *empirical balance* is measured under a stated play policy (for example, uniform random
45: moves) and is the sense in which this variant is defended.
46: _Avoid_: Fairness

(End of file - total 46 lines)

# Tic-Tac-Toe, No Draws

A two-player tic-tac-toe variant whose entire reason to exist is that every game ends with a
winner: X moves first and must complete a line, and a board that fills with no line is awarded
to O.

## Language

**Board**:
The 3×3 grid of nine cells; together with whose turn it is, the whole state of a game.
_Avoid_: Grid, field

**Mark**:
An X or an O occupying a cell. X always moves first, so X places on moves 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9, and
O on moves 2, 4, 6 and 8.
_Avoid_: Piece, token, stone

**Line**:
Any of the eight triples of cells — three rows, three columns, two diagonals — in which a line
win can be completed. Use "row", "column" and "diagonal" only when the orientation matters.

display.text:
# Tic-Tac-Toe, No Draws

A two-player tic-tac-toe variant whose entire reason to exist is that every game ends with a
winner: X moves first and must complete a line, and a board that fills with no line is awarded
to O.

## Language

**Board**:
The 3×3 grid of nine cells; together with whose turn it is, the whole state of a game.
_Avoid_: Grid, field

**Mark**:
An X or an O occupying a cell. X always moves first, so X places on moves 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9, and
O on moves 2, 4, 6 and 8.
_Avoid_: Piece, token, stone

**Line**:
Any of the eight triples of cells — three rows, three columns, two diagonals — in which a line
win can be completed. Use "row", "column" and "diagonal" only when the orientation matters.
_Avoid_: Three-in-a-row (as a name for the cells themselves)

**Line win**:
A player wins by placing a mark that completes a line of three of their own marks.
_Avoid_: Normal win, standard win

**Fill win**:
O wins because the board reaches nine marks with no line. At most one fill win can occur in a
game, and it is always X that has just moved, so a fill win is equivalently "the ninth move
loses".
_Avoid_: Draw-tiebreak, board-full win, stalemate

**Draw**:
A terminal position with no winner. This variant exists to make draws unreachable; a draw is
never a runtime outcome and must never be presented as one.
_Avoid_: Tie, stalemate

**Terminal**:
A position in which the game has ended — by either a line win or a fill win.

**Balance**:
Closeness of the two players' win rates. Two senses must not be conflated: *perfect-play
balance* is impossible in any no-draw variant, because exactly one player has a forced win,
while *empirical balance* is measured under a stated play policy (for example, uniform random
moves) and is the sense in which this variant is defended.
_Avoid_: Fairness

1: # No-draw variants of 3x3 tic-tac-toe: exhaustive solver evidence and source review
2: 
3: Research note, 2026-09-21. Scope: this file answers one design question — can two-player 3x3
4: tic-tac-toe (X and O alternating, no passing) be modified so that (MUST) no terminal state is a
5: draw and (MUST) every line of play terminates, with (NICE) a simple rule and similar first/second
6: win rates. It is evidence for a later `docs/RULES.md` / `docs/DESIGN.md`, not a decision.
7: 
8: **Method.** Part 1 is primary evidence produced here: a stdlib-only Python program that
9: *exhaustively enumerates the complete game tree* for each rule set (every legal move sequence,
10: stopping at terminal positions). Nothing is sampled. Leaf counts are exact; the uniform-random and
11: greedy outcome distributions are computed by exact rational dynamic programming, not simulation.
12: Exploration of this finite tree is therefore a proof over all play, not evidence from a sample.
13: The solver is in the appendix; every number below is reproduced by `python3 solver.py`.
14: 
15: Cell numbering used throughout:
16: 
17: ```
18: 0 1 2
19: 3 4 5
20: 6 7 8
21: ```
22: 
23: X moves first, except rule F, where O is pre-placed on the centre before X's first move.
24: 
25: **Interpretations fixed here** (the brief left these open):
26: 
27: - A move that both completes a line and fills the board is resolved as a *line* result; the line
28:   check happens on the move. This only matters for B and C.
29: - Length is the number of moves made after the starting position (for F, the pre-placed stone is
30:   not counted).
31: - "Random play" means each player chooses uniformly among *legal moves*. This gives different
32:   outcome probabilities from the "share of terminal sequences", because a terminal sequence at
33:   the end of a long path is less likely than one on a short path. Both are reported.
34: - "Greedy" means: take an immediate win if one exists; otherwise choose uniformly among moves
35:   after which the opponent has no immediate win; otherwise choose uniformly among all legal moves.
36:   "Immediate win" is evaluated with each rule's own terminal test.
37: 
38: ---
39: 
40: ## 1. Comparison table (all candidates)
41: 
42: "Random" is the exact move-uniform probability split (X% / O% / draw%); "leaves" is the share of
43: terminal sequences (the framing behind the classic 255,168). "Greedy" is the exact split under the
44: greedy policy. Perfect play is the minimax value; winning first moves are the opening cells (rules
45: with a pre-placed stone list only empty cells).
46: 
47: | # | Rule (delta from standard) | Sentences | Draws? | Max len | Perfect play | Random (move-uniform; leaves) | Greedy | Verdict |
48: |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
49: | — | **Standard**: own 3-in-a-row wins; lineless full board is a draw | 3 | yes, 18.06% of leaves | 9 | draw | X 58.5 / O 28.8 / D 12.7; leaves 51.4 / 30.5 / 18.1 | X 31.1 / O 17.4 / D 51.5 | reject: draws |
50: | A | standard + "**last mover wins a lineless full board**" (= X wins a full board) | 4 | **no** | 9 | **X**, all 9 openings | X 71.2 / O 28.8; leaves 69.5 / 30.5 | X 82.6 / O 17.4 | viable but X-dominant; simplest possible fix |
51: | B | standard + "**last mover loses a lineless full board**" (= O wins a full board) | 4 | **no** | 9 | **O**, no winning opening | X 58.5 / O 41.5; leaves 51.4 / 48.6 | X 31.1 / O 68.9 | **strongest simple candidate**; near-even casual play; perfect play O |
52: | C | misère (own line loses) + "last mover wins a lineless full board" | 4 | **no** | 9 | **X**, centre (4) only | X 41.5 / O 58.5; leaves 48.6 / 51.4 | X 26.5 / O 73.5 | viable; balanced casual play; known X mirror win |
53: | D | misère + "last mover loses a lineless full board" | 4 | **no** | 9 | **O**, no winning opening | X 28.8 / O 71.2; leaves 30.5 / 69.5 | X 13.7 / O 86.3 | reject: dominated by B |
54: | E | a move wins by making **any** line fully occupied, whatever the symbols | 3 | **no** | **7** | **X**, all 9 openings | X 51.6 / O 48.4; leaves 44.6 / 55.4 | X 100 / O 0 | reject: rule is unintuitive; greedy is degenerate |
55: | F(i) | O pre-placed on centre + "last mover wins a full board" | 5 | **no** | 8 | **O**, no winning opening | X 19.3 / O 80.7; leaves 21.7 / 78.3 | X 4.2 / O 95.8 | reject: badly O-dominant |
56: | F(ii) | O pre-placed on centre + "last mover loses a full board" | 5 | **no** | 8 | **X**, corners (0,2,6,8) | X 30.7 / O 69.3; leaves 39.5 / 60.5 | X 70.0 / O 30.0 | reject: handicap does not balance |
57: | G | Maker–Breaker: X wins by an X line, O wins a filled board with no X line | 5 | **no by definition** | 9 | **X**, centre + corners | X 77.8 / O 22.2; leaves 71.0 / 29.0 | X 34.1 / O 65.9 | viable reference; asymmetric goals, not classic tic-tac-toe |
58: | H | single-board Notakto: **both players place X**; completing a line loses | 3 | **no** | **7** | **X**, centre (4) only | first 48.4 / second 51.6; leaves 55.4 / 44.6 | first 62.8 / second 37.2 | **simplest rule and best random-play balance**; but single-symbol and first player has a known forced win |
59: 
60: Reference row (not a candidate, used to check the literature): misère with **no** tiebreak is a
61: draw with perfect play (X 28.8 / O 58.5 / D 12.7 move-uniform; leaf split X 30.5 / O 51.4 / D
62: 18.1); only the centre opening survives, every other first move loses for X.
63: 
64: Dominance summary: **B dominates A** on balance (same tree; the tiebreak is given to the player
65: who is behind under random play rather than ahead); **B dominates D and F(i)** (same or better
66: balance, simpler rule, same forced winner O); **D is the mirror-image worst case** of B. E and G
67: are no-draw by construction but change the character of the game more than B/C. H is the simplest
68: and most balanced empirically, but it is X-only.
69: 
70: ---
71: 
72: ## 2. Part 1 results in detail
73: 
74: ### 2.1 Standard baseline (confirmation)
75: 
76: Exhaustive enumeration reproduces the classic numbers exactly:
77: 
78: - 255,168 terminal sequences [1]: X wins 131,184 [2], O wins 77,904 [3], draws 46,080 [4].
79: - Leaf shares: X 51.411%, O 30.530%, draw 18.059%.
80: - Move-uniform random play: X 58.492%, O 28.810%, draw 12.698%.
81: - Perfect play: draw. All nine first moves have value "draw"; there is no winning first move.
82: - Max length 9; mean length over leaves 8.2545; uniform expectation 7.6262.
83: - 5,478 distinct reachable (board, turn) states; 549,946 nodes in the unfolded game tree.
84: - Length distribution of terminal sequences: 5 moves: 1,440; 6: 5,328; 7: 47,952; 8: 72,576;
85:   9: 127,872.
86: - Distinct terminal boards: 958 — 626 with an X line, 316 with an O line, **16 lineless full
87:   boards**; no board has both lines as a terminal state. This matches the UCI "Tic-Tac-Toe
88:   Endgame" database of 958 legal endgame boards [5].
89: - Of the 126 full 5X/4O boards, 110 contain at least one line and 16 contain none (the 16 draws).
90: 
91: ### 2.2 The 16 lineless full boards, and why they force a design decision
92: 
93: All 16 lineless full boards are reachable in normal play; each is the terminal position of exactly
94: 2,880 complete games, and 16 × 2,880 = 46,080 = the classic draw count. The boards are listed with
95: their sequence counts in the appendix output. This is the crux of the whole exercise: under the
96: standard win condition there are 46,080 reachable terminal positions (18.06% of all terminal
97: sequences) in which *neither player has won*, so **any variant that keeps the standard win
98: condition is forced to add a tiebreak for the filled board** (A, B, F) **or to change the win
99: condition** so that lineless full boards can no longer be terminal states (misère C/D, any-line E,
100: Maker–Breaker G, Notakto H). There is no third option.
101: 
102: ### 2.3 Termination (all candidates)
103: 
104: Termination is structural, not probabilistic. A move occupies one previously empty cell; there is
105: no passing, no capture and no move that keeps the stone count equal. The solver asserts for every
106: edge of every tree that the child has exactly one more stone than its parent, so the reachable
107: state graph is a DAG graded by stone count: **no reachable cycle exists in any candidate**, and no
108: line of play can exceed 9 moves (E and H are bounded by 7, F by 8; see the table). The solver has
109: no recursion-depth or cycle guard because none is needed, and the exhaustive DFS terminated for
110: every rule.
111: 
112: ### 2.4 Notes on the per-rule results
113: 
114: - **A** is the standard tree with all 46,080 draw leaves relabelled as X wins: X 177,264 /
115:   O 77,904. Perfect play is an X win from every opening (X's standard drawing strategy now wins).
116: - **B** relabels the 46,080 draws as O wins: X 131,184 / O 123,984. Perfect play is an O win:
117:   O's standard defensive strategy prevents X from ever completing a line, so the game ends either
118:   with O's line or a filled board, both O wins.
119: - **C** relabels misère's 46,080 draw leaves as X wins: X 123,984 / O 131,184. Perfect play X
120:   with the centre as the unique winning opening, matching the known centre + 180-degree mirror
121:   strategy [7]; see the mirror check below.
122: - **D** relabels them as O wins: X 77,904 / O 177,264. Perfect play O.
123: - **E** has a much smaller tree (max length 7) because any line that becomes fully occupied ends
124:   the game, including mixed X/O lines. X can win as early as move 3 (X at 0, O at 1, X at 2
125:   completes the top row) and O as early as move 4. Perfect play X from every opening; greedy play
126:   is a pure race in which X wins 100% of greedy-consistent lines, which shows how brittle the
127:   rule is under simple play.
128: - **F**: with O pre-placed, X has 5 stones and O 4, so the full-board last mover is X. F(i)
129:   (fill = X win) is a large O win; F(ii) (fill = O win) is an X win in which only the four corners
130:   are winning first moves, and O's free centre does not compensate. Greedy play flips the sign of
131:   F(i) vs F(ii) (X 4.2% vs 70.0%), so the handicap variant's outcome is dominated by the tiebreak,
132:   not by the handicap.
133: - **G** is Maker–Breaker 3x3 [8, 9]: Maker X wins with centre or any corner as a winning first
134:   move, exactly matching the published statement "the center vertex or any corner vertex is a
135:   winning first move for Maker" [8]. Under uniform random play X wins 77.8%, but under the greedy
136:   policy Breaker wins 65.9% of the time: blocking is easy and forking is hard, so Maker's
137:   advantage is real but not robust to weak play.
138: - **H** is single-board Notakto [6]: first player wins, unique winning first move is the centre,
139:   matching the published centre + knight's-move strategy; any other first move loses. Max length
140:   7, because any 7 occupied cells of the 3x3 board contain a line (two empty cells cannot block
141:   all eight lines), so the board can never fill and the game always ends by move 7.
142: 
143: ### 2.5 Uniform random vs greedy vs leaves (why all three are reported)
144: 
145: The three "casual play" measures disagree, and the disagreement is informative. For B, the
146: move-uniform split is X 58.5 / O 41.5 but the leaf split is X 51.4 / O 48.6: long games are less
147: likely, and O's wins happen on average later. Under greedy play B is O-favoured (X 31.1), because
148: greedy players block lines and steer games to filled boards, which B awards to O. Anyone reading
149: these numbers to judge "balance" must say which distribution they mean. The move-uniform
150: distribution is the one a bored human approximates; the greedy distribution is the one a
151: beginner who knows "win or block" approximates.
152: 
153: ### 2.6 Swap (pie) rule check
154: 
155: With the pie rule, X places one stone and O may either play on or swap (take the stone and hand the
156: move back). This was solved exhaustively for A and B, for all nine openings:
157: 
158: - Rule A: O can force a win for every opening (if A's value favours the player who did not move,
159:   O swaps and wins).
160: - Rule B: O can force a win for every opening (O simply plays on and wins).
161: 
162: So the pie rule does not produce theoretical balance in either candidate; it hands the forced win
163: to the second player. See §3.6 for the general argument and its sources.
164: 
165: ---
166: 
167: ## 3. Part 2: literature (primary sources)
168: 
169: Accessed 2026-09-21. Where a claim's owner could not be traced I say so in §4.
170: 
171: ### 3.1 Classic game count and split
172: 
173: The oldest traceable owner of the numbers is Jim Ferry's computation, recorded in OEIS:
174: 
175: - **A061526**, *Number of complete games of n X n tic-tac-toe*: `1, 24, 255168, ...` — a(3) =
176:   255,168 [1].
177: - **A061527**, *won by X*: a(3) = 131,184 [2].
178: - **A061528**, *won by O*: a(3) = 77,904 [3].
179: - **A061529**, *ending in a draw*: a(3) = 46,080 [4].
180: 
181: All four are attributed to "Jim Ferry (jferry(AT)alum.mit.edu), May 04 2001", citing his page
182: "n X n tic-tac-toe (Mathematica programs followed by results)". These are the oldest owning
183: records I found; the number is widely repeated afterwards (e.g. an arXiv note on game-tree
184: estimation uses 255,168 and the split, citing a personal page [16]). I could not trace a
185: pre-2001 published owner. My own enumeration reproduces all four numbers exactly.
186: 
187: ### 3.2 Perfect-play value of standard 3x3
188: 
189: Standard 3x3 is a draw with perfect play. I could not trace a single owning publication for this
190: folklore result: modern papers state it without proof (e.g. "The normal version of tic-tac-toe is
191: a solved game. It always ends up with draw if both players play their best" [7]) and textbooks
192: treat it as the standard example. Rely on the exhaustive minimax in the appendix: value = draw,
193: all nine openings draw. Cited sources: [7] states it; the computation here proves it.
194: 
195: ### 3.3 The 958 terminal positions and the 16 lineless full boards
196: 
197: The UCI "Tic-Tac-Toe Endgame" database [5] is a complete set of legal endgame boards: "This
198: database encodes the complete set of possible board configurations at the end of tic-tac-toe
199: games... Number of Instances: 958 (legal tic-tac-toe endgame boards)... About 65.3% are positive
200: (i.e., wins for x)". The 16 draws within those 958, and the fact that every one is reachable, are
201: established by my own exhaustive enumeration (16 boards, 46,080 game sequences, 2,880 each). The
202: UCI file itself only labels positive/negative, so the 626/316/16 split is my classification of its
203: board set; it agrees with the 626 = 0.653 × 958 count implied by the dataset.
204: 
205: ### 3.4 Misère tic-tac-toe (completing your own line loses)
206: 
207: Junan Pan, *Move first, and become unbeatable: Strategy study of different Tic-tac-toe*,
208: arXiv:2208.06795 (preprint) [7]:
209: 
210: > "The first player can always force a draw if he claims the center for the first move and then
211: > choose the square opposite of his opponent's choice. The first player always loses if he claims
212: > edge or corner first, because there is always a winning strategy for his opponent in that case."
213: 
214: > "To be emphasized, the only unbeatable way for the first player is described as above. If he
215: > starts with edge or corner, he always loses the game when facing a qualified opponent."
216: 
217: My exhaustive check of the strategy: X opens centre and thereafter plays the 180-degree rotation
218: of O's last move. Over all 360 legal O reply sequences in the untiebroken misère game, the result
219: is X 168 wins / O 0 wins / 192 draws — X never loses, and the perfect-play value is a draw, with
220: the centre the unique non-losing first move (0–3,5–8 all lose for X). If the lineless full board
221: is awarded to X (rule C), the same strategy wins all 360 lines; if it is awarded to O (rule D), O
222: wins 192 of the 360. So the misère game is a perfect-play draw, and every no-draw tiebreak converts
223: it into an all-or-nothing result; the mirror strategy is the reason C is a forced X win.
224: 
225: ### 3.5 Notakto (both players place X, completing a line loses)
226: 
227: Plambeck & Whitehead, *The Secrets of Notakto: Winning at X-only Tic-Tac-Toe*, arXiv:1301.1672 [6],
228: quote the origin of the single-board result from the MathOverflow "Neutral tic tac toe" thread:
229: 
230: > "In the 3x3 misere game, the first player wins by playing in the center, and then wherever the
231: > second player plays, the first player plays a knight's move away from that."
232: 
233: and Kevin Buzzard's observation:
234: 
235: > "The reason any move other than the centre loses for [the first player to move] in the 3x3 game
236: > is that [the second player] can respond with a move diametrically opposite [the first player's]
237: > initial move. This makes the centre square unplayable, and then player two just plays the '180
238: > degree rotation' strategy which clearly wins."
239: 
240: The paper's own contribution is the disjunctive (multi-board) misère-quotient analysis; the
241: single-board case is exactly the game solved here as rule H. My exhaustive solve agrees on both
242: points: first player wins, unique winning first move = centre (4), and every other first move is a
243: second-player win. The paper's 18-element misère quotient for multi-board play was **not**
244: re-verified here.
245: 
246: ### 3.6 Zermelo determinacy, and why perfect-play balance is impossible
247: 
248: The result usually called Zermelo's theorem was published as E. Zermelo, *Über eine Anwendung der
249: Mengenlehre auf die Theorie des Schachspiels*, Proc. Fifth International Congress of
250: Mathematicians (Cambridge 1912), CUP, 1913, 501–504 [10]; an English translation is in Schwalbe &
251: Walker, *Zermelo and the Early History of Game Theory*, Games and Economic Behavior 34(1), 2001,
252: 123–137 [11]. A modern restatement: "in any such game either the first player has a winning
253: strategy, or the second player has a winning strategy, or both have unbeatable strategies"
254: (Amir & Evstigneev, *On Zermelo's theorem*, Journal of Dynamics and Games 4(3), 2017 [12]).
255: 
256: **Corollary used here.** In a finite perfect-information game with no draws, the third case is
257: impossible, so exactly one player has a forced win. A "50/50" perfect-play split cannot exist in
258: any no-draw variant; perfect-play win rates are 100/0 in favour of whichever side has the forced
259: win. "Balance" in the brief's sense can therefore only be *empirical* (random/greedy play, as in
260: the table) or a count of winning openings. Every candidate here has a forced winner: A, C, E, G, H
261: favour the first player; B, D, F(i) favour the second; F(ii) favours the first.
262: 
263: ### 3.7 Pie/swap rule
264: 
265: The swap rule in Hex: after the first player's opening stone, the second player may instead swap
266: sides and take that stone. V. Anshelevich, *The Game of Hex: An Automatic Theorem Proving Approach
267: to Game Programming*, AAAI-2000, describes the opening move "also known as the swap rule" [14]. A
268: review of Hayward & Toft, *Hex: The Full Story*, in the Notices of the AMS 68(8), 2021 [15], says:
269: 
270: > "Normally pieces cannot be moved but one important exception used by most players is called the
271: > swap rule. On their first move the second player may move normally, or choose to swap their
272: > piece with that placed by the first player. This encourages the first player to only choose a
273: > moderately strong first move and so reduces any advantage of going first."
274: 
275: Gale's 1979 Monthly paper [13] owns Hex's no-draw property and its equivalence to the Brouwer
276: fixed-point theorem ("Hex... cannot end in a draw", opening line; the paper is a scan I could not
277: text-search). Whether Gale 1979 is also the owner of the swap rule — as the brief suggests — is
278: **unverified**; the earliest swap-rule reference I could confirm is the Hex literature above.
279: 
280: **The no-draw fairness argument, derived here and verified exhaustively.** In a symmetric no-draw
281: game with the pie rule, after X's opening stone at cell *c* the position is (by Zermelo) a forced
282: win for exactly one of the two roles: the player to move (O) or the player owning the stone (X).
283: If O is winning, O plays on; if X is winning, O swaps and takes the owner's role, which is then
284: winning. Either way, O has a forced win. Exhaustive solving confirms this for A and B: O can force
285: a win for every one of the nine openings. So the pie rule does not create theoretical fairness in a
286: no-draw game; it moves the forced win from the first player to the second. Its practical value is
287: that the first player must pick an opening that is neither too strong nor too weak, which balances
288: the *empirical* difficulty rather than the game-theoretic value.
289: 
290: ---
291: 
292: ## 4. Verdicts per candidate
293: 
294: | Candidate | Keep? | Reason |
295: |---|---|---|
296: | Standard | reject | 46,080 draw terminals (18.06% of sequences); fails the MUST |
297: | A | keep (second tier) | Simplest possible no-draw fix (one sentence); terminates by 9; but X wins 69.5% of leaves and every opening is a forced X win, so casual play is lopsided and skilled play is decided at move 1 |
298: | B | **keep (leading simple candidate)** | One sentence; no draws; terminates by 9; closest to even under both casual measures (leaves 51.4/48.6, move-uniform 58.5/41.5); caveat: perfect play is an O win, and greedy play favours O 68.9%, so "even" means even for near-random play, not for competent O |
299: | C | keep (alternative) | No draws; balanced casual play (leaves 48.6/51.4); but the misère wording is longer, and X has a short, teachable forced win (centre + 180-degree mirror) verified over all O replies |
300: | D | reject | Same forced winner as B (O) with much worse balance (28.8/71.2 move-uniform; greedy 13.7/86.3). Dominated by B |
301: | E | reject | No draws and very short games (max 7), but "win by making any line fully occupied" allows winning with a mixed line, is unlike tic-tac-toe, and greedy play is a degenerate X race (100%) |
302: | F(i) | reject | O 80.7% move-uniform, 95.8% greedy; handicap plus tiebreak is two extra rules and badly unbalanced. Dominated by B |
303: | F(ii) | reject | Extra pre-placement rule; perfect play X (corners only) and greedy X 70%, so the handicap does not produce balance; outcome is driven by the fill tiebreak |
304: | G | keep (reference) | No draws by definition; Maker X forced win; but asymmetric goals (O cannot win by a line) and greedy play favours Breaker 65.9%; useful as the formal "maker–breaker" option, less recognisable as tic-tac-toe |
305: | H | **keep (alternative, best casual balance)** | Simplest rule of all ("both players place X; the first to complete a line loses"), no draws, ends by move 7, near-even random play (first 48.4 / second 51.6); caveats: single-symbol (stretches "X and O alternating"), and first player has the known centre + knight's-move forced win [6] |
306: 
307: Shortlist for `docs/RULES.md`, in order of how well they fit "simple + recognisably tic-tac-toe +
308: balanced": **B**, then **A** (simplest wording, worse balance), then **H** (simplest rule, but
309: X-only), then **C** (misère flavour, balanced, but a known forced win for X). B and C are mirror
310: images in casual balance; B dominates D and the F variants.
311: 
312: ---

314: ## 5. Solver code (stdlib-only Python 3)
315: 
316: Save as `solver.py` and run `python3 solver.py`.
317: 
318: ```python
319: #!/usr/bin/env python3
320: """
321: no_draw_ttt.py -- exhaustive solvers for 3x3 tic-tac-toe no-draw rule sets.
322: 
323: Standard library only. Every number printed by this script is obtained by
324: enumerating the complete game tree (every legal sequence of moves, stopping
325: at terminal positions). Nothing is sampled.
326: 
327: Cell numbering:
328:     0 1 2
329:     3 4 5
330:     6 7 8
331: X moves first (rule F excepted: O is pre-placed on the centre).
332: 
333: Each rule is a function (board, last_mover) -> (terminal?, winner|None).
334: """
335: 
336: from fractions import Fraction
337: from functools import lru_cache
338: from itertools import combinations
339: 
340: EMPTY, X, O = 0, 1, 2
341: SYM = {X: "X", O: "O", None: "draw"}
342: 
343: 
344: def other(p):
345:     return O if p == X else X
346: 
347: 
348: LINES = ((0, 1, 2), (3, 4, 5), (6, 7, 8),
349:          (0, 3, 6), (1, 4, 7), (2, 5, 8),
350:          (0, 4, 8), (2, 4, 6))
351: 
352: 
353: def mono(b, p):
354:     return any(b[i] == p and b[j] == p and b[k] == p for i, j, k in LINES)
355: 
356: 
357: def any_full_line(b):
358:     return any(b[i] != EMPTY and b[j] != EMPTY and b[k] != EMPTY
359:                for i, j, k in LINES)
360: 
361: 
362: def board_full(b):
363:     return all(c != EMPTY for c in b)
364: 
365: 
366: def nstones(b):
367:     return sum(1 for c in b if c != EMPTY)
368: 
369: 
370: # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
371: # Terminal rules: (board, last_mover) -> (terminal?, winner or None)
372: # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
373: 
374: def R_standard_draw(b, last):
375:     """Classic tic-tac-toe: a lineless full board is a draw."""
376:     if mono(b, X):
377:         return True, X
378:     if mono(b, O):
379:         return True, O
380:     if board_full(b):
381:         return True, None
382:     return False, None
383: 
384: 
385: def R_standard_fill_wins(b, last):
386:     """Rule A: standard lines; full board with no line -> last mover wins."""
387:     if mono(b, X):
388:         return True, X
389:     if mono(b, O):
390:         return True, O
391:     if board_full(b):
392:         return True, last
393:     return False, None
394: 
395: 
396: def R_standard_fill_loses(b, last):
397:     """Rule B: standard lines; full board with no line -> last mover loses."""
398:     if mono(b, X):
399:         return True, X
400:     if mono(b, O):
401:         return True, O
402:     if board_full(b):
403:         return True, other(last)
404:     return False, None
405: 
406: 
407: def R_misere_fill_wins(b, last):
408:     """Rule C: completing your own line loses; full board -> last mover wins."""
409:     if mono(b, last):
410:         return True, other(last)
411:     if mono(b, other(last)):        # unreachable in play; defensive
412:         return True, last
413:     if board_full(b):
414:         return True, last
415:     return False, None
416: 
417: 
418: def R_misere_fill_loses(b, last):
419:     """Rule D: completing your own line loses; full board -> last mover loses."""
420:     if mono(b, last):
421:         return True, other(last)
422:     if mono(b, other(last)):        # unreachable in play; defensive
423:         return True, last
424:     if board_full(b):
425:         return True, other(last)
426:     return False, None
427: 
428: 
429: def R_any_line(b, last):
430:     """Rule E: a move making any line fully occupied wins, whatever the symbols."""
431:     if any_full_line(b):
432:         return True, last
433:     return False, None
434: 
435: 
436: def R_misere_draw(b, last):
437:     """Misere with no fill tiebreak: a lineless full board is a draw."""
438:     if mono(b, last):
439:         return True, other(last)
440:     if mono(b, other(last)):        # unreachable in play; defensive
441:         return True, last
442:     if board_full(b):
443:         return True, None
444:     return False, None
445: 
446: 
447: def R_maker_breaker(b, last):
448:     """Rule G: X wins with an X line; O wins a filled board with no X line."""
449:     if mono(b, X):
450:         return True, X
451:     if board_full(b):
452:         return True, O
453:     return False, None
454: 
455: 
456: def R_notakto(b, last):
457:     """Rule H (Notakto, single board): both players place X; whoever
458:     completes a line of X's loses."""
459:     if mono(b, X):
460:         return True, other(last)
461:     return False, None
462: 
463: 
464: EMPTY9 = (EMPTY,) * 9
465: F_START = (EMPTY, EMPTY, EMPTY, EMPTY, O, EMPTY, EMPTY, EMPTY, EMPTY)
466: 
467: 
468: def value_function(rule, pieces=None):
469:     """Minimax value of any position: X, O or None (draw)."""
470:     pieces = pieces or {X: X, O: O}
471: 
472:     @lru_cache(maxsize=None)
473:     def value(b, turn):
474:         term, w = rule(b, other(turn))
475:         if term:
476:             return w
477:         vals = set()
478:         p = pieces[turn]
479:         for i in range(9):
480:             if b[i] == EMPTY:
481:                 vals.add(value(b[:i] + (p,) + b[i + 1:], other(turn)))
482:         if turn in vals:
483:             return turn
484:         if None in vals:
485:             return None
486:         return other(turn)
487:     return value
488: 
489: 
490: def solve(rule, start=EMPTY9, start_turn=X, pieces=None):
491:     """Full exhaustive analysis of one rule set from one starting position."""
492:     pieces = pieces or {X: X, O: O}
493:     s0 = nstones(start)
494: 
495:     # (1) complete tree: terminal-leaf counts, exact lengths, and the exact
496:     #     outcome distribution under uniform random play.  Memo key is
497:     #     (board, turn); the previous mover is always other(turn).
498:     @lru_cache(maxsize=None)
499:     def rec(b, turn):
500:         term, w = rule(b, other(turn))
501:         if term:
502:             L = nstones(b) - s0
503:             counts = {X: 0, O: 0, None: 0}
504:             counts[w] = 1
505:             probs = {X: Fraction(0), O: Fraction(0), None: Fraction(0)}
506:             probs[w] = Fraction(1)
507:             return counts, L, L, probs, Fraction(L), 1
508:         legal = [i for i in range(9) if b[i] == EMPTY]
509:         assert legal, ("non-terminal full board reached: rule must declare "
510:                        "a full board terminal")
511:         m = len(legal)
512:         counts = {X: 0, O: 0, None: 0}
513:         probs = {X: Fraction(0), O: Fraction(0), None: Fraction(0)}
514:         mx = 0
515:         slen = 0
516:         elen = Fraction(0)
517:         nstates = 0
518:         for i in legal:
519:             nb = b[:i] + (pieces[turn],) + b[i + 1:]
520:             assert nstones(nb) == nstones(b) + 1      # graded DAG: no cycles
521:             c2, m2, s2, p2, e2, n2 = rec(nb, other(turn))
522:             for k2 in counts:
523:                 counts[k2] += c2[k2]
524:             mx = max(mx, m2)
525:             slen += s2
526:             elen += e2 / m
527:             nstates += n2
528:             for k2 in probs:
529:                 probs[k2] += p2[k2] / m
530:         return counts, mx, slen, probs, elen, nstates + 1
531: 
532:     counts, max_len, sum_len, prob, exp_len, nstates = rec(start, start_turn)
533:     total = counts[X] + counts[O] + counts[None]
534:     distinct_states = rec.cache_info().currsize
535: 
536:     # (2) exact outcome distribution under the greedy policy:
537:     #     win now if possible, else block the opponent's immediate win,
538:     #     else uniform at random.  Ties inside each set are uniform.
539:     @lru_cache(maxsize=None)
540:     def greedy(b, turn):
541:         term, w = rule(b, other(turn))
542:         if term:
543:             L = nstones(b) - s0
544:             counts_ = {X: 0, O: 0, None: 0}
545:             counts_[w] = 1
546:             probs_ = {X: Fraction(0), O: Fraction(0), None: Fraction(0)}
547:             probs_[w] = Fraction(1)
548:             return counts_, L, Fraction(L), probs_
549: 
550:         def play(bb, i, p):
551:             return bb[:i] + (pieces[p],) + bb[i + 1:]
552: 
553:         legal = [i for i in range(9) if b[i] == EMPTY]
554:         assert legal, ("non-terminal full board reached: rule must declare "
555:                        "a full board terminal")
556:         wins = []
557:         for i in legal:
558:             term2, w2 = rule(play(b, i, turn), turn)
559:             if term2 and w2 == turn:
560:                 wins.append(i)
561:         if wins:
562:             cand = wins
563:         else:
564:             opp = other(turn)
565:             safe = []
566:             for i in legal:
567:                 nb = play(b, i, turn)
568:                 term2, w2 = rule(nb, turn)
569:                 if term2:
570:                     continue            # move ends the game without winning
571:                 threat = False
572:                 for j in range(9):
573:                     if nb[j] == EMPTY:
574:                         term3, w3 = rule(play(nb, j, opp), opp)
575:                         if term3 and w3 == opp:
576:                             threat = True
577:                             break
578:                 if not threat:
579:                     safe.append(i)
580:             cand = safe if safe else legal
581:         m = len(cand)
582:         counts_ = {X: 0, O: 0, None: 0}
583:         probs_ = {X: Fraction(0), O: Fraction(0), None: Fraction(0)}
584:         exp_ = Fraction(0)
585:         mx_ = 0
586:         for i in cand:
587:             c2, m2, e2, p2 = greedy(play(b, i, turn), other(turn))
588:             for k2 in counts_:
589:                 counts_[k2] += c2[k2]
590:             for k2 in probs_:
591:                 probs_[k2] += p2[k2] / m
592:             exp_ += e2 / m
593:             mx_ = max(mx_, m2)
594:         return counts_, mx_, exp_, probs_
595: 
596:     gcounts, gmax, gexp, gprob = greedy(start, start_turn)
597: 
598:     value = value_function(rule, pieces)
599:     first_values = {}
600:     for i in range(9):
601:         if start[i] == EMPTY:
602:             nb = start[:i] + (pieces[start_turn],) + start[i + 1:]
603:             first_values[i] = value(nb, other(start_turn))
604: 
605:     return {
606:         "counts": counts, "total": total, "max_len": max_len,
607:         "mean_len": Fraction(sum_len, total), "exp_len": exp_len,
608:         "prob": prob, "states": distinct_states, "tree_nodes": nstates,
609:         "value": value(start, start_turn),
610:         "first_values": first_values,
611:         "winning_first": sorted(i for i, v in first_values.items()
612:                                 if v == start_turn),
613:         "greedy_counts": gcounts, "greedy_max": gmax, "greedy_mean": gexp,
614:         "greedy_prob": gprob,
615:     }
616: 
617: 
618: def fmt_pct(fr):
619:     return f"{float(fr) * 100:.3f}%"
620: 
621: 
622: def print_report(name, rule, start, start_turn, note, pieces=None):
623:     r = solve(rule, start, start_turn, pieces)
624:     c, t, p = r["counts"], r["total"], r["prob"]
625:     print("=" * 78)
626:     print(name)
627:     if note:
628:         print("  note:", note)
629:     print(f"  terminal lines of play (leaves) ... {t}")
630:     print(f"  X / O / draw leaves ............... {c[X]} / {c[O]} / {c[None]}")
631:     print(f"  leaf shares ....................... X {100 * c[X] / t:.3f}%  "
632:           f"O {100 * c[O] / t:.3f}%  draw {100 * c[None] / t:.3f}%")
633:     print(f"  uniform-random-play probabilities . X {fmt_pct(p[X])}  "
634:           f"O {fmt_pct(p[O])}  draw {fmt_pct(p[None])}")
635:     print(f"  game length: max {r['max_len']}, mean over leaves "
636:           f"{float(r['mean_len']):.4f}, uniform expectation "
637:           f"{float(r['exp_len']):.4f}")
638:     if r["winning_first"]:
639:         print(f"  perfect play ...................... {SYM[r['value']]}; "
640:               f"winning first moves {r['winning_first']}")
641:     else:
642:         print(f"  perfect play ...................... {SYM[r['value']]}; "
643:               f"no winning first move")
644:     fv = " ".join(f"{i}:{SYM[v]}" for i, v in sorted(r["first_values"].items()))
645:     print(f"  first-move values ................. {fv}")
646:     gp, gc = r["greedy_prob"], r["greedy_counts"]
647:     print(f"  greedy policy probabilities ....... X {fmt_pct(gp[X])}  "
648:           f"O {fmt_pct(gp[O])}  draw {fmt_pct(gp[None])}   "
649:           f"(greedy leaves X {gc[X]} / O {gc[O]} / draw {gc[None]})")
650:     print(f"  greedy length: max {r['greedy_max']}, expectation "
651:           f"{float(r['greedy_mean']):.4f}")
652:     print(f"  distinct (board, turn) states ..... {r['states']}   "
653:           f"(unfolded game-tree nodes {r['tree_nodes']})")
654:     return r

709: def swap_check(name, rule):
710:     print("=" * 78)
711:     print(f"SWAP / PIE RULE CHECK: {name}")
712:     print("  X opens at cell c.  'O plays on' = value of ({c:X}, O to move);")
713:     print("  'O swaps' = value of ({c:O}, X to move), i.e. O took the stone.")
714:     value = value_function(rule)
715:     all_second = True
716:     for c in range(9):
717:         b_no = tuple(X if i == c else EMPTY for i in range(9))
718:         b_sw = tuple(O if i == c else EMPTY for i in range(9))
719:         v_no = value(b_no, O)
720:         v_sw = value(b_sw, X)
721:         second_wins = (v_no == O) or (v_sw == O)
722:         all_second &= second_wins
723:         print(f"    c={c}: O plays on -> {SYM[v_no]}; O swaps -> {SYM[v_sw]}; "
724:               f"O can force a win: {second_wins}")
725:     print(f"  second player wins with the swap rule for every opening: "
726:           f"{all_second}")

729: def mirror_check(rule, name):
730:     """X opens on the centre, then always plays the 180-degree rotation of
731:     O's last move.  Enumerate every legal O reply sequence."""
732:     outcomes = {X: 0, O: 0, None: 0}
733: 
734:     def rec(b, turn, last):
735:         term, w = rule(b, other(turn))
736:         if term:
737:             outcomes[w] += 1
738:             return
739:         if turn == X:
740:             m = 8 - last
741:             assert b[m] == EMPTY, (b, last)
742:             rec(b[:m] + (X,) + b[m + 1:], O, m)
743:         else:
744:             for i in range(9):
745:                 if b[i] == EMPTY:
746:                     rec(b[:i] + (O,) + b[i + 1:], X, i)
747: 
748:     b0 = EMPTY9[:4] + (X,) + EMPTY9[5:]
749:     rec(b0, O, 4)
750:     tot = sum(outcomes.values())
751:     print(f"  mirror strategy vs {name}: exhaustive over all O replies")
752:     print(f"    (X centre, then rotate O's last move 180 degrees)")
753:     print(f"    X wins {outcomes[X]}, O wins {outcomes[O]}, draws "
754:           f"{outcomes[None]}  (total {tot})")
